text: Every MPI program starts with {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Init}\) }} before any other MPI call, and ends with {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Finalize}\) }}, which frees everything MPI was using.
extra: No MPI calls before Init or after Finalize. Passing NULL, NULL to Init is fine.

text: You start 4 processes. Each one calls {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Comm\_size}\) }} and learns there are 4, then calls {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Comm\_rank}\) }} and learns its own ID, from 0 to 3.
extra: Both calls take the communicator \(\mathrm{MPI\_COMM\_WORLD}\), the group of every process you started. The rank works like a process ID.

text: Every MPI process runs the {{c1::same program}}. An if statement on {{c2::rank}} decides what each one actually does.
extra: In hello world, rank 0 receives and prints while every other rank sends a greeting. The textbook calls this style SPMD.

text: Shipping data over a network is slow, so MPI pays off when each process spends much more time {{c1::computing}} than {{c2::communicating}}.
extra: A render farm is the lecture's example. Each machine renders whole frames, which take a long time compared to sending the scene data.

text: A receive only matches a message sent on the same {{c1::communicator}}, with the same {{c2::tag}}, from the expected {{c3::source}} rank.
extra: If any one of those is off, the receive never completes.

text: Two messages from the same sender carry the same type of data, but one is for printing and one is for computing. You tell them apart with a different {{c1::tag}}.
extra: The tag is a nonnegative int. Assignment 2 uses tags the same way to separate message types.

text: Only the {{c1::receiver}} can use wildcards like \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\) and \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_TAG}\). There is {{c2::no}} wildcard for the communicator.
extra: A sender always names a real destination rank and a real tag.

text: A manager receives with \(\mathrm{MPI\_ANY\_SOURCE}\). To find out who sent the message, it reads {{c1::\(\mathrm{status.MPI\_SOURCE}\) }}. To find the actual tag, it reads {{c2::\(\mathrm{status.MPI\_TAG}\) }}.
extra: You need a real \(\mathrm{MPI\_Status}\) variable for this. Passing \(\mathrm{MPI\_STATUS\_IGNORE}\) throws the information away.

text: The manager asked for up to 256 chars, but the message may be shorter. It calls {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Get\_count}\) }} with the status and the datatype to learn how many actually arrived.
extra: The count is not a field in the status. This is study guide practice question 2, answer A.

text: If rank 1 sends you two messages, the first one arrives first, because MPI messages are {{c1::nonovertaking}}. Messages from {{c2::different}} senders can arrive in any order.
extra: So a receive loop that waits for rank 1, then 2, then 3 may sit waiting even though rank 3 already finished.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\) {{c1::always blocks}} until a matching message arrives. If the send is missing, or its tag or rank does not match, the process {{c2::hangs}} forever.
extra: A mismatch can also make the receive match the wrong send. A send that blocks while waiting for a receive can hang too.

text: When \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) returns, you can reuse the buffer, but you {{c1::do not know}} whether the message was delivered yet. MPI may have {{c2::buffered}} it and moved on.
extra: Whether a send buffers or blocks depends on the MPI implementation. Small messages usually get buffered.

text: Only rank {{c1::0}} can read stdin, so it reads the input and passes it to the other ranks. Every rank can print, but the order of their output is {{c2::unpredictable}}.
extra: Lines from different ranks can come out in any order or even cut into each other.

text: A collective like Reduce or Bcast must be called by {{c1::every}} process in the communicator. Collectives match by communicator and {{c2::call order}}, not by tags.
extra: Point-to-point calls like Send and Recv involve just two processes and match by tag and rank. Matching a Reduce on one rank with a Recv on another is an error.

text: Rank 0 reads a, b, and n. Instead of a loop of sends, it calls {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\) }}, and every process in the communicator ends up with the {{c2::same}} values.
extra: All ranks make the same Bcast call. The buffer is the input on the root and the output everywhere else.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) combines one value from every process with an operator like \(\mathrm{MPI\_SUM}\), and the result lands {{c1::only on the destination}} process.
extra: Other operators include \(\mathrm{MPI\_PROD}\), \(\mathrm{MPI\_MIN}\), and \(\mathrm{MPI\_MAX}\). With a count above 1, arrays get combined element by element.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) does not have every process send straight to the root. It combines partial results in a {{c1::tree}}, so the work of adding is spread over many processes.
extra: The MPI implementation picks the exact pattern for you. You just make the one call.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Allreduce}\) works like Reduce, but the combined result goes to {{c1::every process}}. That is why its call has {{c2::no destination}} argument.
extra: Lecture 10 also calls it a butterfly reduction. Use it when every rank needs the total for its next step.

text: Rank 0 has the whole vector, and each process only needs its own slice. {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Scatter}\) }} splits the array and sends each process {{c2::one chunk}}, rank 0 included.
extra: Bcast sends everyone the same full data. Scatter sends everyone a different piece. The send count is the amount going to each process, not the total.

text: {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Gather}\) }} is the reverse of Scatter. Every process sends its chunk, and only the {{c2::destination}} process ends up with the assembled array.
extra: A typical use is gathering results on rank 0 so it can print them. The receive count is the amount from each process, not the total.

text: Your ranks sit on different machines over a slow network, and you need the sum of \(g(a[i])\). Each rank should {{c1::sum its own block}} locally, then combine with {{c2::one \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) }}.
extra: This is study guide practice question 1, answer D. The trapezoid program in Lecture 11 does the same thing with its local integrals.
